title: Rewarding More Is Better for Soliciting Help, Yet More So for Cash Than for Goods

source.title: Rewarding More Is Better for Soliciting Help, Yet More So for Cash Than for Goods: Revisiting and Reframing the Tale of Two Markets With Replications and Extensions of Heyman and Ariely (2004)
source.authors: Hirotaka Imada, Wan Fei Chan, Yuk Ki Ng, Lee Hing Man, Mei Sze Wong, Bo Ley Cheng, and Gilad Feldman

studies.title: Study 1 · Between-person comparison
studies.description: US MTurk participants each rated one scenario. Includes perceived joy and regret.

studies.title: Study 2 · Within-person comparison
studies.description: UK Prolific participants rated all eight scenarios. The no-payment baseline always came first.

fields.label: Research question
fields.value: When you ask for help moving a sofa, does raising the reward change how likely an average person is expected to help? Is that difference larger for cash than for goods?

fields.label: What this paper revisits
fields.value: Two preregistered studies revisit Study 1 of Heyman and Ariely (2004), which distinguished monetary and social exchange. The newer paper also varies whether no payment is explicitly mentioned and compares designs in which people see one versus all conditions.

fields.label: Helping predictions (H1, H1a–c, H2)
fields.value: Reward size should matter more for cash than for candy. Medium cash should raise expected helping, the two candy levels should produce similar ratings, no payment without mention should outperform low cash, and putting a price on candy should produce a cash-like pattern.

nodes.title: What did they expect for joy?

fields.label: Joy predictions (H3, H3a–b, H4)
fields.value: Study 1 predicted that reward form and level would interact for perceived joy. Table 2 predicts a rise for cash and no change for candy. The discussion also describes a rise for price-tagged candy as a prediction. The authors expected higher joy overall for candy than for cash or price-tagged candy. Regret was exploratory.

fields.label: Reward types and controls
fields.value: The six payment conditions cross low and medium amounts with cash, candy, and candy with a stated price. Two controls either omit payment information or explicitly say there is no payment. The first is the main reference condition.

fields.label: Study designs
fields.value: Study 1 compares people assigned one scenario. Study 2 compares the same person across eight scenarios, with the no-payment-without-mention control always first.

fields.label: Study 1 sample
fields.value: 2,203 US participants recruited through Amazon Mechanical Turk.

fields.label: Study 2 sample
fields.value: 999 UK participants recruited through Prolific Academic.

fields.label: Sample size and exclusions
fields.value: The researchers recruited up to their budget because they could not use the original paper’s effect estimates for power calculations. They report no data exclusions.

fields.label: Sofa-moving vignette
fields.value: The same request to help load a sofa into a van is paired with one of eight offers. The cash amounts were $0.50 and $5. Candy was a bar or a box of chocolate; the $5 price-tagged candy used a chocolate bar. The two no-payment conditions vary only in mentioning that no payment would be given.

fields.label: Exact study materials
fields.value: The original Qualtrics surveys are pinned in the runnable protocol as group_a.qsf (Study 1) and group_b.qsf (Study 2). Table 3 summarizes the conditions; the deposited surveys provide the participant-facing items.

fields.label: Participant experience
fields.value: After consent, participants were assigned one of eight scenarios and rated how likely the average person would help. They then rated perceived joy from helping and regret from declining to help, with those two questions randomized in order.

fields.label: Participant experience
fields.value: After consent, participants rated the no-payment scenario that did not mention payment first, then rated the other seven scenarios in randomized order. The study omitted joy and regret.

fields.label: Expected helping
fields.value: The main outcome is an 11-point rating of how likely the average person would be to help, from 1 (not likely at all) to 11 (will help for sure). Study 2’s preregistration manuscript said 7 points, but the authors report that the survey used the preregistered materials’ 11-point scale.

fields.label: Perceived affect
fields.value: Study 1 also measured perceived joy if someone helped and regret if someone did not help. The original survey displayed 0–10 for these questions and coded responses as 1–11 for analysis. Regret was exploratory.

fields.label: Analysis plan
fields.value: The six paid conditions enter a 3 × 2 between-person ANOVA. Planned pairwise tests use estimated marginal means and Tukey adjustment. The four-condition comparison that includes cash and no-payment conditions used Welch’s ANOVA after an unequal-variances check.

fields.label: Analysis plan
fields.value: The six paid conditions enter a 3 × 2 repeated-measures ANOVA. The authors report Greenhouse–Geisser corrections where sphericity was violated. Planned contrasts use paired t-tests on raw means with unadjusted p-values.

fields.label: Reward form by amount (H1)
fields.value: The authors report a reward form by amount interaction for expected helping, F(2, 1643) = 31.96, p < .001. The runnable protocol scores individual contrasts and a descriptive cash-versus-candy difference. The reported omnibus test is outside the protocol’s scoring scope.

fields.label: Cash level (H1a)
fields.value: Expected helping rose from 3.63 with low cash to 7.15 with medium cash (low minus medium d = −1.25, p < .001).

fields.label: Candy level (H1b)
fields.value: Expected helping also rose for candy (d = −0.43, p < .001), contrary to the predicted null result.

fields.label: Priced candy (H2)
fields.value: A higher priced-candy offer increased expected helping (d = −0.37, p < .001). The size of this increase was closer to candy than to cash. This did not support H2’s predicted cash-like pattern.

fields.label: No payment compared with low cash (H1c)
fields.value: The no-payment-without-mention control rated higher than low cash (d = 0.90, p < .001). Mentioning no payment did not yield a statistically clear difference from omitting payment (p = .09).

fields.label: Perceived joy (H3–H4)
fields.value: The overall joy interaction was unsupported. Medium cash was associated with higher perceived joy than low cash. Adjusted level comparisons for candy and priced candy were inconclusive. Candy was rated as yielding more joy than cash and priced candy. Table 4 and the supplement disagree on the candy-versus-priced-candy mean difference.

fields.label: Additional prespecified comparisons
fields.value: Priced candy compared with cash had d = −0.03 (p = .89) and compared with candy had d = −0.15 (p = .04). The no-payment-without-mention control compared with low candy had d = 0.38 and compared with low priced candy had d = 0.50 (both p < .001).

fields.label: Exploratory findings
fields.value: The authors report a Bayes factor of 20,841.04 in favor of a nonzero candy amount effect on expected helping. The paper plots regret in Figure 2 and points to auxiliary analyses on OSF.

fields.label: Reward form by amount (H1)
fields.value: The authors report a reward form by amount interaction for expected helping, F(1.90, 1900.34) = 428.58, p < .001. The runnable protocol scores individual contrasts. The reported omnibus test is outside the protocol’s scoring scope.

fields.label: Cash level (H1a)
fields.value: Expected helping rose from 5.35 with low cash to 7.98 with medium cash (low minus medium d = −1.30, p < .001).

fields.label: Candy level (H1b)
fields.value: Expected helping also rose for candy (d = −0.87, p < .001), contrary to the predicted null result.

fields.label: Priced candy (H2)
fields.value: A higher priced-candy offer increased expected helping (d = −0.80, p < .001). The effect was closer to candy than to cash. This did not support H2’s predicted cash-like pattern.

fields.label: No payment compared with low cash (H1c)
fields.value: The no-payment-without-mention control rated slightly below low cash (d = −0.11, p < .001), the opposite of Study 1. Mentioning no payment raised the rating compared with omitting payment (reported d = 0.25, p < .001).

fields.label: Additional prespecified comparisons
fields.value: Priced candy compared with cash had d = −0.55 and compared with candy had d = −0.15. The no-payment-without-mention control compared with low candy had d = −0.30 and compared with low priced candy had d = −0.18 (all p < .001).

nodes.title: What held across the two studies?

fields.label: Reward size mattered across forms
fields.value: Expected helping increased with reward size for cash, candy, and priced candy. The cash effect was larger. Both studies found that the priced-candy pattern was closer to candy than cash. The medium priced reward was a chocolate bar and the medium unpriced reward was a chocolate box, so the comparison does not isolate the effect of showing a price.

fields.label: The controls behaved differently
fields.value: Low cash compared with no payment reversed across the two studies. The authors offer possible explanations involving design and the fixed-first control in Study 2. These explanations were not separately tested.

fields.label: Expected rather than observed behavior
fields.value: The vignette measures judgments about hypothetical helping. Real-world helping and effects of larger incentives are outside the measured scope.

issues.title: Original control wording unavailable
issues.reason: The 2022 supplement says the original article gave inadequate information about how it phrased the no-payment control.
issues.impact: Limits comparison with the 2004 original; the two 2022 replication surveys are available.
issues.suggestedAction: Consult the original authors or archived original study materials if exact historical replication is needed.

issues.title: Original follow-up tests unspecified
issues.reason: The 2022 supplement reports that the original follow-up tests could not be reconstructed from its account.
issues.impact: Limits comparison with the 2004 original; the two 2022 replication surveys are available.
issues.suggestedAction: Consult the original authors or archived original study materials if exact historical replication is needed.

issues.title: Exact participant payment unspecified
issues.reason: Table 1 describes compensation as nominal payment in both studies. It does not give an amount.
issues.impact: An exact recruitment-compensation match cannot be established from the paper. Vignette payment amounts are reported.
issues.suggestedAction: Consult the authors or the original recruitment listings if the exact amount is needed.

issues.title: The discussion reverses the Study 2 cash comparison
issues.reason: The discussion describes expected helping as higher for low cash than medium cash. Table 4 and the Results report the reverse direction.
issues.impact: The Program uses the direction supported by the reported results.
issues.suggestedAction: Compare Table 4 and the Study 2 results with the discussion.
